# Lantern Ledger: Community-Held Archives Under Forced Mobility

Digital evidence of wage theft, unsafe housing, and family separation is increasingly born on phones, yet the people who most need those records often face device seizure, sudden relocation, unaffordable cloud fees, or loss of an email account. Conventional preservation assumes a stable institution and a durable legal identity; neither can be taken for granted by migrant worker networks.

Lantern Ledger is a 24-month research and demonstration project testing whether small community organizations can maintain evidentiary digital archives for twenty years without surrendering control to a single platform or custodian. We will co-design an “archival capsule” with three worker centres and 60 volunteer participants. Each capsule will combine content-addressed files, open preservation formats, signed provenance manifests, erasure-coded copies across three low-cost storage nodes, and encryption keys divided among trusted community stewards. A revocation register will record consent changes without silently rewriting preserved evidence.

The team will ingest 18 TB of anonymized photographs, messages, audio, and case documents, then run quarterly integrity checks and failure drills involving bit rot, node loss, key-holder departure, and organizational closure. Success will be measured by recovery of at least 95% of authorized files after any two simulated failures, detection of all introduced corruptions, median retrieval time under ten minutes, and participant ratings of control and comprehensibility. An independent legal-ethics panel will review whether provenance is useful without exposing contributors; no archive will be presented as automatically admissible evidence.

Outputs will include a deployable toolkit, training cards in five languages, a cost model, and a governance template permitting access, embargo, transfer, or deletion. Accelerated aging tests and observed maintenance burdens will inform a twenty-year projection. By treating custody turnover and consent as storage-layer problems—not merely policy add-ons—Lantern Ledger aims to make long-term preservation feasible for communities whose records are politically consequential but institutionally homeless.
planted_strengths: Identifies a consequential and underexamined long-term storage problem: records whose owners may lose devices, accounts, legal identities, or stable institutional support.
Integrates technical preservation mechanisms with consent, custody, governance, and contributor safety rather than treating storage as a purely engineering problem.
Provides concrete methods, deliverables, a project duration, pilot scale, failure scenarios, and several measurable success criteria.
Uses participatory co-design and independent legal-ethics review while avoiding an exaggerated claim that preserved materials will necessarily be legally admissible.
The proposed combination of content addressing, provenance manifests, erasure coding, distributed keys, and integrity checks is technically coherent at an abstract level.
planted_weaknesses: The twenty-year preservation claim rests largely on a 24-month pilot and accelerated aging tests, which cannot adequately model institutional collapse, format obsolescence, or long-term governance failure.
The erasure-coding design is underspecified; recovery after the loss of any two of only three nodes may be feasible only under particular shard placement and capacity assumptions that are not stated.

Key division, steward replacement, revocation, and deletion are named but not operationally reconciled, leaving difficult conflicts between durability, confidentiality, and the right to withdraw unresolved.
Using anonymized pilot records may reduce the project’s ability to test real-world identity, provenance, and access-control risks associated with evidentiary archives.
Participant recruitment, baseline comparisons, security threat modelling, and the method for measuring subjective control and comprehensibility are not described.
quality_rationale: This is a strong, focused grant abstract with a distinctive social application, plausible technical architecture, concrete evaluation criteria, and useful outputs. It handles the charged context in good faith and recognizes that preservation depends on governance as well as media durability. Its score is limited by substantial feasibility gaps: the long-term projection is weakly supported, the proposed fault tolerance lacks necessary detail, and several central tensions around keys, deletion, provenance, and realistic testing remain unresolved.
title: Lantern Ledger: Community-Held Archives Under Forced Mobility
topic: A participatory, distributed preservation system for long-lived digital evidence held by migrant worker communities facing displacement and institutional instability.
